title: Data governance
blurb: Roles, operating models, definitions and quality: the vocabulary and moves for running governance without hand-waving.

cards.prompt: Data owner, data steward, data custodian: which is accountable for the data, which looks after it day to day, and which runs the systems it lives in?
cards.answer: Owner: accountable for the data asset. Approves definitions, access and quality targets. Usually a business leader. Steward: responsible day to day for definitions, quality rules, metadata and issue triage, acting for the owner. A subject-matter expert. Custodian: technical custody. Storage, security controls, backups, implementing the rules. Usually IT or a DBA.
points: Owner = accountability and decision rights, one per asset
Steward = day-to-day responsibility for meaning and quality
Custodian = technical operation and controls, not business meaning
Terms vary across frameworks, so define them in the charter

cards.prompt: In the DAMA-DMBOK wheel, which knowledge area sits at the hub, and what does that placement say?
cards.answer: Data governance. It sits at the centre of the other ten knowledge areas because it gives direction and oversight to all of them, which keeps them consistent with each other.
cards.why: The ten around it: architecture; modeling and design; storage and operations; security; integration and interoperability; documents and content; reference and master data; warehousing and business intelligence; metadata; data quality. You don't need to recite them.

cards.prompt: What is the core move of Seiner's 'non-invasive data governance'?
cards.answer: Formalize the accountability people already have for the data they define, produce and use, instead of inventing new roles and new work. Governance recognizes existing stewards and adds structure around them.
points: Recognize existing behavior rather than assign new duties
Anyone who defines, produces or uses data already has a stewardship relationship to it
Lower adoption cost, which matters where people are stretched
cards.source: Robert S. Seiner, Non-Invasive Data Governance (2014)

cards.prompt: A customer record has a real, correctly formatted postal code, but it belongs to a different town than the one the customer lives in. Which quality dimension failed: validity or accuracy?
cards.answer: Accuracy. The code passes the format and domain rules, so it is valid, but it doesn't match reality.
cards.why: Validity = conforms to format and domain rules. Accuracy = matches the real-world thing. A validation rule can't catch an accuracy error; that takes a reference source or verification.
cards.source: DAMA UK, The Six Primary Dimensions for Data Quality Assessment (2013)

cards.prompt: Name the six DAMA UK data quality dimensions.
cards.answer: Completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, validity, accuracy, consistency.

cards.prompt: What is a critical data element, and why does governance start there?
cards.answer: A data element whose quality materially affects key decisions, operations, or legal and regulatory obligations. You can't govern everything at once. CDEs focus definitions, quality rules and stewardship where errors cost the most.
points: Defined by the consequence of error, not by volume
Gives governance a finite, prioritized scope
Owners and quality rules get attached to CDEs first

cards.prompt: Centralized, decentralized or federated: which governance operating model fits an organization with a small central data office, and what does it look like?
cards.answer: Federated (hub and spoke). The central office sets standards, policy and tools and convenes people. Business units keep ownership and do the work through local stewards. A council or committee connects the hub to the spokes.
points: Central office: standards, policy, tools, convening
Business units own their data and execute
A council or community links hub and spokes
Pure centralization doesn't scale with a small office; pure decentralization fragments definitions

cards.prompt: A department head says: 'We don't have time to name a data steward.' You need their core operational data governed. What do you propose?
cards.answer: Someone already answers questions about that data, so name that person and formalize what they already do rather than adding a new job. Shrink the ask to a handful of critical fields and an hour or two a month. Tie it to a pain they feel, such as fewer ad hoc requests or numbers they can defend. Start with one visible use case, and go through the sponsor or council only if this stalls.
points: Reframe as recognizing an existing role (non-invasive)
Shrink the ask: a few critical data elements, time-boxed
Show what they get back (fewer requests, defensible numbers)
Start from one painful, visible use case
Escalate through the executive sponsor or council only if needed

cards.prompt: RACI: what do the letters stand for, and what is the one hard rule?
cards.answer: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. Exactly one A per task or decision.

cards.prompt: Dehghani's four principles of data mesh.
cards.answer: Domain-oriented ownership; data as a product; a self-serve data platform; federated computational governance.
cards.why: The governance principle: global standards are agreed jointly and enforced automatically by the platform, while domains own their data products.

cards.prompt: Policy, standard, procedure, guideline: what does each layer of a governance document set say?
cards.answer: A policy states what must be true and why, at a level leadership approves and rarely changes. A standard makes it specific and checkable (naming rules, required metadata fields, retention periods). A procedure is the step-by-step how. A guideline is recommended practice, not mandatory.
points: Policy: intent and mandate, approved by leadership, stable
Standard: specific, measurable requirements
Procedure: steps to comply
Guideline: advice, not mandatory
Keeping detail out of policy means the details can change without re-approval

cards.prompt: Two departments define the same metric differently (say, 'active customer'), and each definition is right for its own purpose. What should governance do?
cards.answer: Don't force a single definition when the purposes really differ. Give each a distinct qualified name, document both in the glossary with an owner and a derivation, and say which one is authoritative for cross-organization reporting. Only push for convergence where a shared number is needed, and make sure every report states which definition it uses.
points: Different purposes can justify different definitions
Disambiguate with distinct, qualified names
Document each with owner and derivation
Designate one as authoritative for shared reporting
Converge only where a shared number is needed; reports name their definition

cards.prompt: Data governance vs data management: what's the difference?
cards.answer: Governance decides and oversees: it sets the decision rights, policies and standards for data, and checks that they're followed. Management executes: it's the work of carrying those decisions out across the data lifecycle, such as modeling, storing, integrating, securing and improving data. DMBOK defines data governance as the exercise of authority and control (planning, monitoring and enforcement) over the management of data assets.
points: Governance: decision rights, policies, standards and oversight
Management: executing those decisions across the lifecycle
Governance makes sure data is managed properly; it doesn't do the managing
DMBOK: authority and control over the management of data assets

cards.prompt: What is the data lifecycle, and why manage data across all of it?
cards.answer: Data has a life: it's planned, designed, created or obtained, stored and maintained, used, enhanced, and eventually disposed of. Each stage has its own costs and risks. Quality is cheapest to build in at creation, value only arises at use, and data kept past its useful life adds cost and risk, so disposal needs a plan too.
points: Stages run from planning and creation, through use, to disposal
Quality is cheapest to build in at creation
Value only arises when data is used
Keeping data past its useful life adds cost and risk

cards.prompt: DMBOK's data management maturity levels, 1 to 5.
cards.answer: 1 Initial (ad hoc). 2 Repeatable. 3 Defined. 4 Managed. 5 Optimized. Level 0 means no capability at all.
cards.why: Why it matters: a maturity assessment is for baselining and for finding the next sensible step. Chasing a level number for its own sake misses the point.

cards.prompt: How do most data quality frameworks define 'quality'?
cards.answer: Fitness for use: data is high quality when it meets the needs of the people and processes that use it.
cards.why: So quality is relative to a purpose. The same dataset can be fit for a trend report and unfit for billing, which is why quality rules should come from what data consumers need.
cards.source: Wang & Strong, Beyond Accuracy: What Data Quality Means to Data Consumers (1996); Juran
